moduleDoc:
Kinematics of RoboDojo's two ARX-X5 arms, computed in the host: full pose, no RPC.

RPent's RoboDojo environment exposes one IK call, ``solve_ik_position``: a target position, a
few candidate orientations (the current one, the starting one, 25 degree tilts of the current
one about world x and y), the one needing the least joint motion.  Nothing can ask for an
orientation, and the tilts accumulate: an arm sent away and back to its starting position by
``move_to`` came back rotated by 47 to 52 degrees.  The simulator's own full-pose action path
(``<arm>_ee_pose``) swings the arm when its IK diverges.

So the host solves IK itself.  The chain is the benchmark's URDF (``Assets/Robots/x5/X5A.urdf``,
joints ``joint1`` .. ``joint6``, ending at ``link6``), and each arm's base pose was fitted to
113 (joint angles, reported end-effector pose) pairs recorded in four episodes: the
reported ``<arm>_ee_pose`` is exactly the pose of ``link6`` in the world (0.00 mm and 0.000
degrees of residual), with the bases on the table edge at x = -0.30 / +0.30, y = -0.45,
z = 0.765, turned 90 degrees about z.  The solution is commanded as joint angles, the action
path RPent's ``move_to`` uses for its own IK solutions.

Frames.  ``link6``'s x axis is the gripper's pointing direction (wrist to fingertips) and the
two fingers close along its y axis.  At the start both grippers point away from the robot
(+y in the world) with the fingers side by side (closing along world x).  :data:`TCP_OFFSET`
places the grasp point, between the fingertips, on the pointing axis.

Orientation for people: ``pitch`` is how far the pointing direction is below the horizontal
(0 level, 90 straight down), ``yaw`` its heading on the table (0 away from the robot, +90 to
the robot's left, i.e. world -x), ``roll`` the turn of the fingers about the pointing direction
(0 as at the start).  The rotation is ``Rz(90 + yaw) @ Ry(pitch) @ Rx(roll)``; pointing straight
down, ``yaw`` and ``roll`` both turn about the vertical, and :func:`angles` reports roll 0.

moduleDoc:
A RoboDojo toolkit that needs nothing but an environment.

RPent's ``RoboDojoToolkit`` wraps RPent's simulator bridge and records RPent's artifacts.  Under
RoboDojo's own evaluation client there is no RPent: there is an observation (three colour
images and the robot's state, with a depth image and the cameras' matrices when the client's
configuration switches them on) and an action that takes joint targets.
:class:`NativeToolkit` is what the robot class needs on top of that and no more: the tools of
:mod:`.robodojo_tools` (through the depth image where the observation has one, from colour
alone where it has not), ``segment``, the recorded steps (``view_env_state``, the images and
the cameras' calibration of each step) and the envelope RPent's toolkit wraps a
state-changing tool's result in, which :func:`pyrualean._backend.unwrap` reads.

``env`` is anything with ``get_obs() -> dict`` (``vision`` / ``state`` / ``instruction``),
``step(action) -> (obs, reward, done, info)`` with ``info["status"]`` holding ``step`` and
``step_limit``, and ``get_status()``.  ``sam3_client`` segments an image by words or by a pixel
(RPent's ``Sam3Client`` interface).

moduleDoc:
An object's 3D extent from its masks in colour cameras alone: no depth image.

RoboDojo's evaluation client, as configured, hands a policy three colour images and the
robot's state: depth and camera matrices are switched off in its config.  The cameras' poses
are nevertheless known.  The head
camera never moves, and each wrist camera is bolted to its arm's end-effector link, whose pose
is part of the state (:func:`head_view`, :func:`wrist_view`; the numbers were read off the
simulator once).  So every pixel is a known ray, and an object that stands on a known plane
(the table) can be measured from where the rays of its mask go:

*   A mask in ONE camera says where the object's shadow falls on the table as seen from that
    camera: the object fills some of the space between the camera and that shadow.  How tall it
    is cannot be read from it: a low deep thing and a tall shallow one cast the same shadow.
*   For a height ``h`` there are two readings of one mask.  An upright ``prism``: the table cells
    that are in the shadow and whose column up to ``h`` stays in the mask; for a box or a can
    of that height these cells are its footprint, exactly.  Something that ``hangs`` from that
    height: every cell whose point at ``h`` is in the mask, with as much below it as the mask
    allows, standing on the table or not; that is a bowl from its rim down, or anything wider
    above than below.
*   A SECOND camera that sees the object from elsewhere settles the height: the solid a reading
    describes is projected into it and compared with the object's mask there.  The reading and
    height that match best are taken (:func:`measure`); the hanging one only where it matches
    clearly better, since whatever stands on its own footprint is a prism.  With only one mask
    the height is the tallest prism that still accounts for the whole mask, which is right for
    boxes and cans and a guess for a bowl.

:func:`measure` answers with the world point each pixel of the mask shows on that solid: what a
depth image would have given for an object of that shape.

A wrist camera always sees its own two fingers, and sometimes the other arm.  Those pixels
(:func:`robot_pixels`) are ``unknown`` in that view: what a reading puts behind them counts
neither for nor against it, and a mask that lies on them is the robot's, not the object's.

RoboDojo tools of this library's own, registered on RPent's toolkit at boot.

RPent's RoboDojo toolset moves an arm only by position (``move_to``) and grips one native
action at a time (``set_gripper``); its perception returns one mask centroid and one surface
point.  The tools here are what a program needs on top of that, computed in the host from the
same observations and commanded through the same action path:

``move_pose``    the grasp point to a position AND an orientation, along a straight line,
                 with the host's own IK (:mod:`.robodojo_kinematics`);
``grip``         a full gripper stroke, repeated until the fingers stop, with what they hold;
``locate``       an object's 3D extent, heading and top from its mask and the depth image;
``home``         the joints the episode started with (:func:`home`, kept from before).

Every tool is registered as a stateful (not read-only) tool, so RPent's toolkit records a step
after it like after its own motions.  Each native action is one ``env.step`` and counts against
the episode's budget; a tool stops at the step limit.

moduleDoc:
Between XPolicyLab's two calls and an environment a program steps.

XPolicyLab's evaluation client owns the simulator and asks a policy for actions: it sends an
observation (``update_obs``) and asks what to do (``get_action``).  A PyRUA-Lean episode is the
other way round: a program calls a tool, the tool steps the environment and reads what came
of it.  :class:`Bridge` turns one into the other.  The policy server answers ``get_action``
with the next native action a tool has asked for; the tool's ``step`` returns when the client
has taken it and sent the observation that followed.

A model thinks for minutes between two actions, far longer than the client waits for one
answer, so ``get_action`` never holds the client longer than ``poll_s``: when no tool has
stepped by then it answers :data:`WAIT`, and the adapter's ``deploy.py`` asks again.  An empty
answer means the program has finished.  ``deploy.py`` adds the episode's step count and limit
to each observation (``additional_info["pyrualean"]``) and reports the benchmark's verdict
when the episode is over (the protocol's ``trial_end``, which the server hands to
``on_trial_end``).

An older RoboDojo client's pictures run one observation behind its state (fixed upstream
in 6e3190f).  ``deploy.py`` says which client it is, and the bridge adds to each observation
the state its pictures show (``image_state``: the previous observation's for such a client),
which is what the tools take a wrist camera's pose from; where the client sends the cameras'
matrices, a late picture gets the matrix of the observation before as well.

:class:`PolicyModel` is the object XPolicyLab's policy server serves (its ``Model``);
:func:`serve` runs that server in this process.

RoboDojo through its own evaluation client and XPolicyLab.

The host of ``--robot robodojo_xpl``.  RoboDojo's evaluation runs a policy as two processes
that talk XPolicyLab's websocket protocol: the evaluation client owns the simulator
(``src/eval_client/main.py``), builds the observation (three colour images and the robot's
state; a depth image and the camera matrices where its config switches them on, which this
host does for the client it starts) and counts the task's own action budget; a policy server
answers ``update_obs`` / ``get_action``.  This host is the policy server.  :func:`boot`

*   builds the directory the client runs from (:mod:`.robodojo_client_root`): RoboDojo's
    code and configuration copied, XPolicyLab's code and the adapter
    (``integrations/xpolicylab/PyRUA_Lean``) beside them, ``Assets`` linked;
*   serves a :class:`.xpolicylab_bridge.Bridge` with XPolicyLab's policy server, in a thread;
*   starts the evaluation client on one task and one layout (``scripts/eval_policy.sh``, the
    script RoboDojo's own CLI ends in), which connects to that server;
*   and returns a :class:`.robodojo_native.NativeToolkit` over the bridge once the first
    observation has arrived.

What the client decides stays the client's: when the task is solved it ends the episode at
once, and when the program has finished it judges the scene as it stands
(``backend.conclude()``).  ``Cell.seed`` is the layout; ``eval_seed`` (0, 1 or 2) picks which
of RoboDojo's three layout sets it is taken from.  The one layout is picked the way
XPolicyLab's ``scripts/run_robodojo_layout_range.sh`` picks layouts: a resume manifest that
leaves every other one out.

``ROBODOJO_SOURCE_ROOT``; ``Assets`` in it, or ``ROBODOJO_ASSETS_ROOT``), ``msgpack-numpy``
for both sides and ``websockets >= 13`` for the server.  ``ROBODOJO_XPL_SITE`` may name a
directory with ``common/`` (what both sides lack) and ``server/`` (what only the server may
see): the simulator's environment keeps the websockets it was built with.  Without a
checkout the tree ``rlinf-robodojo-runtime`` ships is used (an older client), with the
XPolicyLab checkout ``--xpolicylab-root`` / ``ROBODOJO_XPOLICYLAB_ROOT`` names.

moduleDoc:
RoboDojo robot API for code policies.

Perception (``segment``, ``back_project``) and the frozen Pi0.5 policy
(``pi0_pick``) are RPent's RoboDojo tools (``robots/robodojo/tools.py``) with
RPent's argument names and defaults.  Motion and grasping are this library's
own (``hosts/robodojo_tools.py``, registered on RPent's toolkit at boot, so they
are executed and recorded like RPent's tools): RPent's toolset moves an arm by
position only and its IK lets the wrist drift, which leaves a program unable to
orient the fingers for a grasp or to bring an arm back to its starting pose,
and RoboDojo counts 45 of its 54 tasks as solved only with both arms back.
``move_to`` solves a full-pose IK in the host (``hosts/robodojo_kinematics.py``,
the benchmark's URDF fitted to the reported poses exactly) and moves the grasp
point along a straight line; ``set_gripper`` (a full stroke that reports what
it holds), ``locate`` (an object's 3D extent from its mask and the depth image)
and ``home`` complete the set.  Only what a program cannot compose from the
others is a primitive: a button press is a ``move_to`` past the surface, a
twist is a ``move_to`` with another ``roll``.  The calling convention is
the library's: a policy is an ordinary Python program that calls these methods
and branches on their typed return values.

RoboDojo is the one robot whose success flag RPent keeps from its planner:
official success is read by the runner after the planner has finished, and no
tool result carries it.  This class keeps that regime, so the code arm sees
what the tool-calling arm sees: it has no ``done`` (``ABSENT_MEMBERS``; the
attribute raises rather than answering a constant False that a
``while not robo.done`` loop would spin on), its ``State`` has no
``terminated`` and no result has a success-of-the-task field.  The host reads
the verdict from the backend when the episode is over.

The docstrings in this module are the model-facing documentation: the prompt
is generated from them (see :mod:`pyrualean.prompt`), so keep them accurate.

symbols.name: RobodojoRobot
symbols.doc:
The RoboDojo dual-arm station: two 6-DoF ARX-X5 arms with parallel grippers at a table.

World frame: x runs across the table (the LEFT arm is at negative x and
appears on the LEFT of the head image), y points away from the robot
towards the far edge of the table, z is up; metres.  Orientations are unit
quaternions ordered [w, x, y, z].  The arms are ``"left"`` and ``"right"``
(``robo.LEFT`` / ``robo.RIGHT``). ``move_to`` names one arm and
holds the other; ``move_both`` moves both on one native action clock.
Choose roles, ordering and recovery in your Python program.

``move_to`` drives an arm's GRASP POINT, the middle of the finger pads
(``state().left.tcp_pos``), to a world position, with an orientation given
in degrees: ``pitch`` is how far the gripper points below the horizontal
(0 level, 90 straight down), ``yaw`` the heading of the pointing direction
on the table (0 away from the robot, +90 towards the robot's left, -90
towards its right) and ``roll`` the turn of the fingers about the pointing
direction (0: side by side, as at the start).  Pointing straight down, the
fingers close along the line at ``yaw`` degrees from +x (counter-clockwise
seen from above): ``locate``'s ``grasp_yaw`` is that line across an
object's narrow side.  The table
surface is at z = 0.765; the arms stand on it at x = -0.30 and +0.30,
y = -0.45.

Two gripper conventions, do not mix them up.  COMMANDS are signed:
``robo.CLOSE`` (1) closes, ``robo.OPEN`` (-1) opens, ``robo.KEEP`` (0)
leaves the gripper as it is.  MEASUREMENTS (``state().left.gripper``,
``Gripper.opening``) are openings: 1.0 = open, 0.0 = closed on nothing.

Every native action (one step of ``move_to``, ``set_gripper`` or
``home``, one VLA action) counts against the episode's
native-action budget; when it is spent the state reports ``truncated``
and motion calls raise ``EpisodeFinished``.  Motion calls block until the
primitive finishes and return a typed result; nothing is queued.

Perception is camera based: a fixed head camera (``cam_head``, the whole
table) and one wrist camera per arm (``cam_left_wrist``,
``cam_right_wrist``), 640x480 each.  ``locate`` finds an object by a text
prompt and measures it in 3D (centre, top, footprint, heading);
``segment`` / ``back_project`` give a mask centroid and the world point at
one pixel.  Object poses are never given.

The frozen Pi0.5 VLA (``pi0_pick``) is a learned dual-arm policy trained on
demonstrations of this benchmark's tasks.

symbols.name: RobodojoRobot.segment
symbols.doc:
Segment an object in the current image of ``camera`` by a text prompt (SAM3).

Args:
    text_prompt: what to find, e.g. ``"the green bottle"``.  Name one
        object by its visible properties.
    camera: ``"cam_head"`` (default), ``"cam_left_wrist"`` or
        ``"cam_right_wrist"``.
    min_score: masks scoring below this are reported as not found.
Returns:
    Segment; when ``found``, pass ``centroid`` (row, col) to
    ``back_project`` with the same camera to get a world point.  The
    mask is the best match for the text, not a guarantee of identity:
    check where it is against the image.
Raises:
    ToolError: the camera image or the SAM3 service is unavailable.

symbols.name: RobodojoRobot.back_project
symbols.doc:
Return the world point seen at one pixel of the current image of ``camera``.

Args:
    row / col: pixel, row 0 at the top, col 0 at the left (images are
        480 rows x 640 cols).
    camera: the camera the pixel was read from (default ``"cam_head"``).
Returns:
    WorldPoint; ``xyz`` is where the camera ray meets the first
    surface.  A pixel on an object's edge or a thin part can land on
    the table or the background behind it: prefer ``Segment.centroid``.
Raises:
    ToolError: pixel out of range, no valid depth there, or the
    camera calibration is missing.
symbols.body:
camera = _camera(camera, self.CAMERAS)
kwargs: dict[str, Any] = {"row": int(row), "col": int(col), "camera": camera}
p = self._readonly("back_project", kwargs)
pixel = p.get("pixel") or (int(row), int(col))
return WorldPoint(
            pixel=(int(pixel[0]), int(pixel[1])),
            xyz=_tuple3(p.get("world_xyz")),

symbols.name: RobodojoRobot.locate
symbols.doc:
Find an object by a text prompt and measure it in 3D.

SAM3 segments the current image of ``camera`` (as ``segment``); every
pixel of the mask is then projected into the world through the depth
image, and the points above the table give the object's centre, top,
footprint and heading.  Nothing moves.

Args:
    text_prompt: one object by its visible properties, e.g. ``"the
        small red cube on the left"``.
    camera: ``"cam_head"`` (default; the whole table),
        ``"cam_left_wrist"`` or ``"cam_right_wrist"`` (close up, from
        the gripper: re-measure before a precise grasp).
    min_score: masks scoring below this are reported as not found.
Returns:
    ObjectPose.  For a top grasp: ``move_to([x, y, top_z + 0.08],
    pitch=90, yaw=grasp_yaw)`` above it, then down to the height to
    hold it at.  The mask is the best match for the text, not proof of
    identity: check it against the image.
Raises:
    ToolError: the camera image or the SAM3 service is unavailable.
symbols.body:
camera = _camera(camera, self.CAMERAS)
prompt = str(text_prompt)
if not prompt.strip():
            raise ValueError("text_prompt must not be empty")
kwargs: dict[str, Any] = {
            "text_prompt": prompt,
            "camera": camera,
p = self._readonly("locate", kwargs)
centroid = p.get("centroid_rc") or ()
center = p.get("center_xyz")
return ObjectPose(
            found=bool(p.get("found")),
            center_xyz=_tuple3(center) if center is not None else None,

symbols.name: RobodojoRobot.pi0_pick
symbols.doc:
Run the frozen Pi0.5 policy closed loop until an arm has lifted something.

The policy was trained on complete demonstrations of this benchmark's
tasks, each under its task instruction: it is a whole-task policy, not
a grasp skill (the name is RPent's).  It receives the three current
camera images, both arms' joint state and an instruction, and drives
BOTH arms for up to ``max_chunks`` chunks of up to 50 native actions
each.  The call returns as soon as its grasp heuristic fires (an arm
went down, came back up at least 0.04 m and has its gripper closed) or
the budget runs out; called again, the policy carries on from the
scene as it then is.

Args:
    prompt: the instruction for the policy.  None (default) uses the
        benchmark's own task instruction (``robo.task``).  An override
        must name the intended object by what distinguishes it (not
        just "pick the bottle") and must not contain template markers
        such as ``<target>``.
    arm: recorded as ``monitored_arm`` only; the policy chooses the arm
        itself and the heuristic watches both.
    max_chunks: upper bound on policy chunks (>= 1).  Each chunk can
        spend 50 native actions of the episode's budget, so the
        default can spend 400.
Returns:
    Pick; ``success`` is a provisional heuristic.  Look at the wrist
    camera of the arm that lifted (``Pick.left`` / ``Pick.right``) to
    confirm that the intended object is held.  A broad task
    instruction may fit several objects and promises no grasp order.
Raises:
    ToolError: the policy service is unavailable or the prompt was
    rejected.

symbols.name: RobodojoRobot.move_to
symbols.doc:
Move one arm's grasp point to a world position, with an orientation.

The grasp point is the middle of the finger pads (``tcp_pos``).  The
library solves the arm's inverse kinematics for the full pose and,
with ``path="auto"``, moves the grasp point along a straight line to
it, about 2.5 cm or 8 degrees per native action; when the line leaves
the arm's reach it swings the joints straight to the solution instead.
Nothing moves when the pose is out of reach or every way there takes
the arm into the table: ``ik_error`` says why.

Args:
    xyz: target grasp-point position [x, y, z], metres.
    arm: ``"left"`` or ``"right"``.  The other arm holds its joints.
    gripper: ``robo.CLOSE`` (1) or ``robo.OPEN`` (-1) to command the
        moving arm's gripper on every action of the motion,
        ``robo.KEEP`` (0) to keep commanding what it was last told (a
        held object stays squeezed).  Keep it closed (1) while
        carrying an object.
    pitch / yaw / roll: the orientation to arrive with, degrees (the
        class docstring defines them).  An angle left None keeps its
        current value, so a plain position move does not turn the
        gripper.  With an EMPTY open gripper the fingers are
        interchangeable, so the pose turned half a turn about the
        pointing direction may be taken when it needs less joint
        travel (``note`` says so; yaw / roll then read 180 off);
        holding something, the pose is taken exactly as asked.
    path: ``"auto"`` (default), ``"line"`` (straight line or nothing)
        or ``"joint"`` (swing the joints: fewer actions, but the grasp
        point does not follow a line: not near objects).
Returns:
    Move; test ``reached`` (within 0.01 m and 5 degrees).  ``blocked``
    means the arm was stopped by something on the way.
Raises:
    ValueError: a malformed argument (nothing is sent).

symbols.name: RobodojoRobot.set_gripper
symbols.doc:
Close or open one gripper, without moving the arms.

The command is repeated until the fingers stop (2 to 10 native
actions).  After a close, ``holding`` tells whether something stopped
the fingers apart and ``width_m`` how wide it is.  Later motions with
``robo.KEEP`` keep commanding what was commanded last, so a held
object stays squeezed and a partial opening stays as it is.

Args:
    arm: ``"left"`` or ``"right"``.
    gripper: ``robo.CLOSE`` (1) or ``robo.OPEN`` (-1).
    opening: with ``robo.OPEN`` only: open to this reading
        (0 < opening <= 1) instead of all the way, e.g. to reach
        between close neighbours.  Something 0.002 + 0.109 x opening
        metres wide then just fits between the fingers.
Returns:
    Gripper.  ``holding`` is not proof that the INTENDED object is
    held: confirm it moves with the arm (wrist camera, or ``locate``
    it again after a lift).

symbols.name: RobodojoRobot.home
symbols.doc:
Return an arm to the joint angles it had when the episode started.

A grasp point lower than 1.0 m first goes straight up by up to 6 cm;
then each native action commands the starting angles directly, so the
arm swings straight back: no IK and no path planning beyond that lift
(clear tall things yourself).  The call returns when every joint is
within 0.01 rad or after 25 actions of the swing.  The gripper keeps
the opening it has; an arm that is not named holds its joints.  Most
tasks count as done only with both arms back where they started.

Args:
    arm: ``"left"``, ``"right"`` or ``"both"`` (default).
Returns:
    Home; test ``reached`` and call again when it is False.

moduleDoc:
The RoboDojo robot under RoboDojo's own evaluation client, through XPolicyLab.

The same robot as ``pyrualean.robodojo`` (the same API, the same tools, the same knowledge
file), served to RoboDojo's evaluation client as an XPolicyLab policy instead of being run on
RPent's simulator bridge: the client owns the simulator and gives the verdict
(:mod:`pyrualean.hosts.xpolicylab_robodojo`).

Its perception reads what ``pyrualean.robodojo`` reads: a depth image and the camera matrices.
RoboDojo's simulator emits both, its released data is RGB-D, and the client's configuration
shipped with them on; they have been off by default since RoboDojo PR 2.  The host switches
them on in the configuration of the client it starts.  Under a client somebody else starts
they have to be on there (``observation.vision.depth`` or ``approximate_depth``,
``intrinsic_matrix``, ``extrinsic_matrix`` in ``env_cfg/<config>.yml`` and the
``distance_to_image_plane`` capture in its camera file); where they are not,
``pyrualean.robodojo_xpl_rgb`` is the robot that needs none of it.

There is no VLA in this host; capability filtering selects ``no-vla`` automatically.

``pyrualean.robodojo_xpl`` is the RoboDojo robot under RoboDojo's own evaluation client with

from its side, and no adapter on the leaderboard reads them.  The robot here is the same
robot with perception that needs no more than that default: ``locate`` measures an object
from its masks in the cameras that see it (:mod:`pyrualean.hosts.robodojo_sight`),
``back_project`` answers for the object under a pixel, ``camera_meta`` is worked out from the
robot's state.  Motion and the gripper are unchanged.

The host is :mod:`pyrualean.hosts.xpolicylab_robodojo_rgb`.  There is no VLA in that host:
capability filtering selects ``no-vla`` automatically.

symbols.name: ObjectSight
symbols.doc:
Outcome of ``locate``: an object measured from its masks in the colour cameras.

found: SAM3 produced a mask scoring at least ``min_score``.
center_xyz: [x, y, z] of the middle of the smallest rectangle around the
    object's footprint, at half its height above the table, metres.  A
    handle, a spout or a tail is part of the footprint and moves the
    middle away from the body's.  None when no 3D measurement was
    possible (see ``note``).
top_z: height of the object's top surface.
height_m: ``top_z`` above the table surface (0.765 m).
length_m / width_m: the long and the short side of the smallest rectangle
    around the footprint.
long_axis_deg: direction of the long side on the table, degrees from +x
    (-90 .. 90); of a square, one of its sides.
grasp_yaw: the ``yaw`` for ``move_to(..., pitch=90, yaw=grasp_yaw)``:
    pointing straight down, the fingers then close across the short side
    (a cube's: across two faces).
views: how many cameras agreed on the measurement.  1: nothing but the
    camera asked saw the object, and its height is a guess (see
    ``locate``); ``note`` says which guess.
score: SAM3 confidence.
centroid: (row, col) of the mask in the image, as ``Segment.centroid``.
area_px: mask pixels.
camera: the camera measured from.
note: what limits the measurement (one camera only; two that agree only
    roughly; the mask is the robot's own arm, or not on the table; too
    flat or too far to measure), else None.

The object is taken to stand on the table.  What other things or the
robot's own arm hide of it is not measured, so a partly hidden object
comes out smaller and off-centre.  A held object is usually not found from
the head camera.
symbols.body: views: int = 1

symbols.doc:
Outcome of ``back_project``: the point seen at one pixel.

xyz: world [x, y, z], metres: where the pixel's ray meets the object under
    the pixel, or the table.
depth_m: distance of that point along the camera's optical axis.
surface: ``"object"`` when the pixel lies on something that could be
    measured, ``"table"`` when the point is on the table top (z = 0.765):
    the pixel shows the table, or something too flat or too far to measure.

symbols.name: RobodojoOfficialColourRobot
symbols.doc:
The RoboDojo dual-arm station: two 6-DoF ARX-X5 arms with parallel grippers at a table.

World frame: x runs across the table (the LEFT arm is at negative x and
appears on the LEFT of the head image), y points away from the robot
towards the far edge of the table, z is up; metres.  Orientations are unit
quaternions ordered [w, x, y, z].  The arms are ``"left"`` and ``"right"``
(``robo.LEFT`` / ``robo.RIGHT``). ``move_to`` names one arm and
holds the other; ``move_both`` moves both on one native action clock.
Choose roles, ordering and recovery in your Python program.

``move_to`` drives an arm's GRASP POINT, the middle of the finger pads
(``state().left.tcp_pos``), to a world position, with an orientation given
in degrees: ``pitch`` is how far the gripper points below the horizontal
(0 level, 90 straight down), ``yaw`` the heading of the pointing direction
on the table (0 away from the robot, +90 towards the robot's left, -90
towards its right) and ``roll`` the turn of the fingers about the pointing
direction (0: side by side, as at the start).  Pointing straight down, the
fingers close along the line at ``yaw`` degrees from +x (counter-clockwise
seen from above): ``locate``'s ``grasp_yaw`` is that line across an
object's narrow side.  The table
surface is at z = 0.765; the arms stand on it at x = -0.30 and +0.30,
y = -0.45.

Two gripper conventions, do not mix them up.  COMMANDS are signed:
``robo.CLOSE`` (1) closes, ``robo.OPEN`` (-1) opens, ``robo.KEEP`` (0)
leaves the gripper as it is.  MEASUREMENTS (``state().left.gripper``,
``Gripper.opening``) are openings: 1.0 = open, 0.0 = closed on nothing.

Every native action (one step of ``move_to``, ``set_gripper`` or
``home``, one VLA action) counts against the episode's
native-action budget; when it is spent the state reports ``truncated``
and motion calls raise ``EpisodeFinished``.  Motion calls block until the
primitive finishes and return a typed result; nothing is queued.

Perception is from colour images alone; there is no depth image.  A fixed
head camera (``cam_head``, the whole table) and one wrist camera per arm
(``cam_left_wrist``, ``cam_right_wrist``), 640x480 each, and where each
one is, is known from the robot's state.  ``locate`` finds an object by a
text prompt and measures it in 3D (centre, top, footprint, heading) from
the cameras that see it: it takes two of them to measure a height.
``segment`` / ``back_project`` give a mask centroid and the world point at
one pixel.  Object poses are never given.

The frozen Pi0.5 VLA (``pi0_pick``) is a learned dual-arm policy trained on
demonstrations of this benchmark's tasks.

symbols.name: RobodojoOfficialColourRobot.camera_meta
symbols.doc:
Return the calibration of one camera at a recorded step as a dict.

Keys: ``shape`` (image shape), ``intrinsic_matrix`` (3x3) and
``extrinsic_matrix`` (4x4 camera-to-world; the camera looks down its
own -z axis with +y up).  The head camera is fixed; a wrist camera
moves with its arm, and its pose is worked out from that arm's state.

symbols.name: RobodojoOfficialColourRobot.back_project
symbols.doc:
Return the world point seen at one pixel of the current image of ``camera``.

There is no depth image, so a pixel alone is only a ray.  The object
under the pixel is segmented from that pixel (SAM3) and measured as
``locate`` measures one, and the answer is where the pixel's ray
meets it.  A pixel on the table top itself gives the point of the
table it shows, exactly.

Args:
    row / col: pixel, row 0 at the top, col 0 at the left (images are
        480 rows x 640 cols).
    camera: the camera the pixel was read from (default ``"cam_head"``).
Returns:
    SeenPoint; check ``surface``.  ``"object"``: ``xyz`` is on the
    object under the pixel, as well as ``locate`` would measure that
    object from this camera and the others that see it.
    ``"table"``: ``xyz`` is on the table top; a pixel that shows
    something too flat or too far to measure also answers so.  A thin
    part in mid-air (a peg, a handle, a cable) is not measured
    reliably: reason from the image and from ``locate`` of the whole
    object instead.
Raises:
    ToolError: pixel out of range, or it looks past the table.
symbols.body:
camera = _camera(camera, self.CAMERAS)
kwargs: dict[str, Any] = {"row": int(row), "col": int(col), "camera": camera}
p = self._readonly("back_project", kwargs)
pixel = p.get("pixel") or (int(row), int(col))
return SeenPoint(
            pixel=(int(pixel[0]), int(pixel[1])),
            xyz=_tuple3(p.get("world_xyz")),

symbols.name: RobodojoOfficialColourRobot.locate
symbols.doc:
Find an object by a text prompt and measure it in 3D from the colour cameras.

SAM3 segments the current image of ``camera`` (as ``segment``); the
same object is then looked for in the other two cameras, and its
height and footprint are those that fit every camera that shows it.
One camera cannot measure a height: a low deep thing and a tall
shallow one look alike from it.  ``views`` says how many cameras
agreed.  Nothing moves.

Args:
    text_prompt: one object by its visible properties, e.g. ``"the
        small red cube on the left"``.
    camera: ``"cam_head"`` (default; the whole table),
        ``"cam_left_wrist"`` or ``"cam_right_wrist"`` (close up, from
        the gripper).
    min_score: masks scoring below this are reported as not found.
Returns:
    ObjectSight.  For a top grasp: ``move_to([x, y, top_z + 0.09],
    pitch=90)`` above it, ``locate`` it again from there (the wrist
    camera then looks down on it and the reading is good to 1-2 mm),
    turn to ``yaw=grasp_yaw`` and go down to the height to hold it
    at.  With ``views >= 2`` and no ``note`` a block, a can, a bowl
    or the body of a bottle is measured to 1-3 mm; a ``note`` that
    the cameras agree only roughly leaves the height uncertain.  With
    ``views == 1`` the height is a guess, the tallest upright shape
    that fits the one image: close for a box or a can, wrong for a
    bowl, a cup or anything wider above than below, and for a tall
    thing that tapers; ``center_xyz`` is then off, along the line
    away from the robot, by about half of what the height is wrong
    by.  An object once measured with ``views >= 2`` keeps that height
    in later calls with the same prompt.  No position comes back
    (``center_xyz`` None, ``note`` says why) for a mask on the robot's
    own arm or on something that is not on the table.  The mask is
    the best match for the text, not proof of identity: check it
    against the image.
Raises:
    ToolError: the camera image or the SAM3 service is unavailable.
symbols.body:
camera = _camera(camera, self.CAMERAS)
prompt = str(text_prompt)
if not prompt.strip():
            raise ValueError("text_prompt must not be empty")
kwargs: dict[str, Any] = {
            "text_prompt": prompt,
            "camera": camera,
p = self._readonly("locate", kwargs)
centroid = p.get("centroid_rc") or ()
center = p.get("center_xyz")
note = p.get("geometry_error") or p.get("height_guess")
return ObjectSight(
            found=bool(p.get("found")),
            center_xyz=_tuple3(center) if center is not None else None,
